extracted.intended_audience: public relations counsels / PR practitioners / communications professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Techniques and standards for planning and executing public-relations campaigns: selecting media, segmenting audiences, timing messages, and recognizing limits of influence. Emphasis on using existing communication channels and tailoring appeals to overlapping group identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match content to public tastes / 'fitness to print'
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers and other media must sell to the public; standards of 'fitness' reflect the point of view of a paper's readership and determine what is printed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance between giving the public what it wants and giving the public what it should want; examples include music, drama and advertising adapting to public taste. Understand the clientele's expectations to maintain circulation and financial success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial selection and winnowing of news
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors sift the day's material and select which facts to print, how much space to give them, what position and emphasis to assign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that selection is constrained by what else happened that day ('What Else Happened That Day?' advertisement). Real news displaces semi-news; when big news breaks, less-sensational items are dropped. Use this to plan timing and prominence.

rubrics_metrics.name: No objective standards — follow conventions and paper traditions
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no purely objective standards for choosing or presenting items; newspapers follow conventions and the traditions of their particular constituencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor headlines, angle, and emphasis to the target publication's audience and customary treatment (example: same-day headlines can present entirely different priorities depending on paper). Study each medium's 'scheme of treatment' before pitching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use established mediums of communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Proponents must utilize existing channels (daily press, magazines, lecture circuits, advertising media, motion pictures, etc.) rather than attempt to build entirely new organs of expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creating new channels (newspapers, radio stations, distribution networks) is costly, slow, and often impractical. Plan campaigns around available, established media to reach majorities and minorities efficiently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target publics that are already prepared or sympathetic
rubrics_metrics.description: A leader's influence depends on an audience already predisposed to his views; sympathy cannot be manufactured from nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalize on groups with common traditions or prior acceptance — e.g., Margaret Sanger speaking to receptive audiences, Madam Curie's reception aided by preparatory education. Avoid addressing deeply hostile groups without groundwork.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limits of PR — the public's internal censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: The average citizen's own mind acts as an efficient censor (e.g., 'logic-proof compartments'); group mind inertia and preconceptions block facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that PR cannot fully overcome entrenched absolutisms; employ impartial analysis and tactical presentation but accept realistic limits on persuasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience subdivision and segmentation (interlapping group formations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Society consists of many overlapping groups; successful campaigns subdivide the audience into component groups that share interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze and organize appeals by groupings (business types, professions, religious or ethnic affiliations). Example: Federation for the Support of Jewish Charities divided appeals to dentists, bankers, theater owners, etc., to mobilize support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor appeals to each group's strongest motives and overlapping identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the multiple identities of individuals (e.g., professional, humanitarian, religious) to craft messages that resonate on more than one axis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appeal to social aspirations, ambitions for leadership, competitive desires, philanthropy, or civic pride depending on the group's strongest levers. Leverage overlap (e.g., business + humanitarian) to broaden acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use broad, fundamental appeals for heterogeneous audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: When addressing very diverse or scattered publics, select appeals rooted in basic values (loyalty, fairness, patriotism, safety) to obtain wide resonance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: railroad poster campaigns appealing to instinctive carefulness; re-employment campaigns for veterans stressing loyalty and fairness. Use simple graphic or emotional prompts for mass comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education and information campaigns to build common consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The method of education by information (creating 'knowledge of national circumstances') is essential to develop a shared basis for opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deploy systematic information, analysis and public education (e.g., Committee on Public Information) to increase understanding and voluntary cooperation. PR often functions as the agent of such informative campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider cost, feasibility, and time when choosing channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Establishing new newspapers, radio stations, or motion-picture distribution is expensive and slow; economic realities constrain channel choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess mechanical, staffing, distribution and promotional costs before attempting new channels; frequently the cost/benefit favors using existing media even for partisan messages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing, freshness, and news context determine prominence
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsworthiness depends on freshness and the day's context; the relative importance assigned by papers affects public thought and character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan releases and events with awareness of competing stories — an engagement photo can be omitted if an earthquake breaks the same day. Aim for timing when 'real news' space is available or craft angles that rise above competing items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial craft can shape perception especially on slow news days
rubrics_metrics.description: When big news is scarce, skilled editing selects semi-news to fill public attention — this selection fixes readers' opinions about country and compatriots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On 'dull' news days, provide well-edited, interesting material that will receive prominent placement and thus disproportionately influence public impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the two-way influence between leaders and the public
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaders and public shape each other: leaders can intensify or dissipate existing sympathy but often cannot create it; the public also molds leaders' reputations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design actions and messages knowing that public reaction constrains leaders (example: Admiral Dewey's loss of affection after an action perceived unfavorably). Use tactics that align leader behavior with public expectations.
